title: Make Love, Not Warcraft

Synopsis[]: The boysdedicate their lives to defeating amad gamerand saving theWorld of Warcraft.
Plot[]: Within the digital realm of Azeroth, Stan, Kyle, and Kenny awaited Cartman's return, the latter claiming a significant biological function had detained him. Their virtual repose was shattered by Randy Marsh's demand for Stan to engage in offline socialization, a request Stan countered with the assertion that online interaction constituted social activity. Rejoining the fray, the trio was summarily dispatched by a high-level player, a duel they hadn't consented to. This digital aggressor proved to be a caricature of a socially awkward individual.

The following day, a call to Blizzard Entertainment's support line revealed the boys' predicament. While the representative acknowledged the forced combat scenario, she hinted at a larger, systemic issue plaguing the game. Within Blizzard's inner sanctum, the gravity of the situation was laid bare: player attrition loomed if these digital slayings continued unabated. The rogue player, it was revealed, had achieved near-mythical status through relentless, around-the-clock gameplay, his power surpassing even that of the Game Masters themselves. "How can we defeat that which has no life?" the CEO lamented.

Meanwhile, Randy, now a WoW player himself, regaled his colleague Nelson with tales of his virtual exploits, only to be felled by the same rogue player who had vanquished his son. In his subterranean lair, Cartman assembled a cadre of male classmates, including Butters, Tweek, and others, to devise a plan to eliminate the rogue player. Butters, confessing his preference for Hello Kitty Island Adventure, was coerced into joining the WoW fray under threat of physical reprisal.

That night, the assembled forces clashed with the rogue player, their initial assault proving futile. Clyde's distraction with adult literature, Cartman's micromanagement of Butters' gameplay, and Randy's unexpected return to the game all contributed to their failure. The Blizzard administrators, observing the carnage, despaired, believing the game's demise was imminent. A chance encounter at the basketball court led Cartman to propose a new strategy: a relentless grind of boar slaying in a non-PvP zone. The goal: accumulate 65 million experience points over seven weeks. A montage, underscored by Paul Stanley's "Live to Win," depicted their arduous, sedentary journey, their physical forms expanding with each digital kill.

The Blizzard staff, witnessing their progress, saw a glimmer of hope. Whispers of the Sword of a Thousand Truths, a legendary weapon of immense power, reached their ears. The weapon, deemed too potent for general use, had been removed from the game, its digital essence stored on a USB flash drive. The belief arose that these dedicated players might be the chosen ones to wield this ultimate weapon.

In Cartman's basement, the final battle commenced. Liane Cartman provided sustenance for the extended engagement. Seventeen hours into the conflict, Kyle succumbed to carpal tunnel syndrome, requiring topical relief from Cartman. Randy, accompanied by Blizzard staff, raced to deliver the Sword of a Thousand Truths, only to find Stan absent. Learning of his whereabouts, they embarked on a frantic search.

At Best Buy, Randy commandeered a computer, logged into his noob account, and, after a crash course in item transfer, bestowed the sword upon Stan. Stan, wielding the legendary blade, confronted the rogue player, whose defenses crumbled under the weapon's power. The combined assault of the group, culminating in Cartman's decisive blow, finally vanquished the digital tyrant.

Randy's dramatic, albeit temporary, demise and subsequent logout marked the end of the battle. The victors celebrated, the game's future secured. As the dust settled, Stan pondered their next move. Cartman's simple answer: "We can finally play the game now." And so they did.
